section.title: Immanuel, the Sign to Ahaz
section.sectionRationale: This movement opens the great block of Immanuel oracles running through chapters 7-12: Ahaz, terrified by a coalition of Aram and Israel, refuses to ask God for a sign of assurance, so the LORD gives one anyway, a child called Immanuel, God with us, alongside a sober warning that Assyria, the very power Ahaz hopes will save him, will instead overrun the land.
section.thesis: When faithless Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, the LORD gives one regardless, a virgin-born son called Immanuel, God with us, a near sign of deliverance from two enemy kings that also opens a horizon toward a far greater fulfillment, even as Ahaz's own faithlessness invites the very Assyrian devastation he sought to avoid.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Ahaz's terror before the Aram-Israel coalition; the LORD's offer of a sign and Ahaz's faithless refusal; the sign of Immanuel given anyway; and the coming Assyrian devastation pictured in stripped land and briers.

units.label: Trees shaken by the wind
units.note: Ahaz terrified before Aram and Israel

verses.text: Now in the days that Ahaz son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, was king of Judah, Rezin king of Aram marched up to wage war against Jerusalem. He was accompanied by Pekah son of Remaliah the king of Israel, but he could not overpower the city.
When it was reported to the house of David that Aram was in league with Ephraim, the hearts of Ahaz and his people trembled like trees in the forest shaken by the wind.
Then the LORD said to Isaiah, “Go out with your son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz at the end of the aqueduct that feeds the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field,
and say to him: Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened over these two smoldering stubs of firewood, over the fierce anger of Rezin and Aram and of the son of Remaliah.
For Aram, along with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has plotted your ruin, saying:
‘Let us invade Judah, terrorize it, and divide it among ourselves. Then we can install the son of Tabeal over it as king.’

But this is what the Lord GOD says: 
‘It will not arise; it will not happen.
For the head of Aram is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people.
The head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you do not stand firm in your {{emunah|faith}}, then you will not stand at all.’”

units.label: A sign refused
units.note: I will not test the LORD

verses.text: Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz, saying,
“Ask for a sign from the LORD your God, whether from the depths of Sheol or the heights of heaven.”
But Ahaz replied, “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.”
Then Isaiah said, “Hear now, O house of David! Is it not enough to try the patience of men? Will you try the patience of my God as well?

units.label: The sign of Immanuel
units.note: the virgin will conceive and bear a son

verses.text: Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the {{almah|virgin}} will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him {{immanuel|Immanuel}}.
By the time He knows enough to reject evil and choose good, He will be eating curds and honey.
For before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste.
The LORD will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father a time unlike any since the day Ephraim separated from Judah, He will bring the king of Assyria.”

units.label: The coming devastation
units.note: briers, thorns, and a shaved land

verses.text: On that day the LORD will whistle to the flies at the farthest streams of the Nile and to the bees in the land of Assyria.

And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines and clefts of the rocks, 
in all the thornbushes and watering holes.
On that day the Lord will use a razor hired from beyond the Euphrates, the king of Assyria, to shave your head and the hair of your legs, and to remove your beard as well.
On that day a man will raise a young cow and two sheep,
and from the abundance of milk they give, he will eat curds; for all who remain in the land will eat curds and honey.
And on that day, in every place that had a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels of silver, only briers and thorns will be found.
Men will go there with bow and arrow, for the land will be covered with briers and thorns.
For fear of the briers and thorns, you will no longer traverse the hills once tilled by the hoe; they will become places for oxen to graze and sheep to trample.

emunah.gloss: To stand firm, be established, from a root also giving us amen. Verse 9 contains a famous Hebrew wordplay, im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu, if you do not stand firm you will not be established, using the same root twice to make trust itself the very ground of stability.

almah.gloss: A young woman of marriageable age, normally presumed to be unmarried and therefore a virgin in ancient Israelite culture, though the word itself emphasizes youth rather than virginity technically. Matthew 1:23 renders it with the Greek parthenos, virgin, applying the sign fully and finally to Mary's miraculous conception of Jesus.

immanuel.gloss: God with us, a name combining the preposition with us and El, God. The name functions as both a sign of assurance to Ahaz's generation and, in its fullest sense, as the very identity of Christ, who is literally God become flesh and dwelling among His people, Matthew 1:23, John 1:14.

basic.context: King Ahaz is terrified because two neighboring kings have joined forces to attack Jerusalem and replace him with their own puppet ruler. God sends Isaiah to reassure Ahaz that this threat will fail, and even offers Ahaz any sign he wants as proof, but Ahaz refuses under a show of false piety. So God gives a sign anyway: a virgin will bear a son called Immanuel, God with us, and before that child is old enough to know right from wrong, both threatening kings will be gone, though a far more dangerous power, Assyria, whom Ahaz secretly hoped would rescue him, will instead devastate the land.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage operates on two horizons at once, a genuinely historical sign for Ahaz's own crisis around 734 BC, and a further, greater fulfillment that Matthew 1:23 explicitly identifies in the virgin birth of Jesus. The honest question readers must face is how one sign can address both a near, immediate need and a distant, climactic one; the pattern, sometimes called prophetic telescoping, appears elsewhere in Scripture and does not require choosing one fulfillment over the other, since both are affirmed by the text and its New Testament application.
basic.originalLanguages: Verse 9 turns on a famous Hebrew wordplay built on one root, aman, standing firm: if you do not stand firm in faith, you will not be established at all, tying trust itself to stability. The almah, young woman, of verse 14 will bear a son called Immanuel, God with us, a name whose full weight is realized only when Matthew identifies the child as Jesus, literally God dwelling among His people in flesh.
basic.typology: Immanuel, God with us, given first as a sign in Ahaz's crisis, becomes the defining identity of Christ Himself, whose incarnation is the ultimate fulfillment of God's presence among His people. The child eating curds and honey, marking a time of judgment and scarcity, also anticipates a pattern where the Messiah's early life is marked by humble, ordinary circumstances even while carrying the weight of ultimate significance.
basic.christ: Matthew 1:22-23 quotes this prophecy directly, declaring it fulfilled in the virgin conception of Jesus by Mary through the Holy Spirit, and explicitly translating Immanuel as God with us. Where Ahaz refused to trust God even when offered any sign he wanted, Jesus is the sign finally given regardless of human unbelief, God Himself coming to dwell among a faithless people, not because they deserved it but because His mercy would not be stopped by their refusal.
basic.god: God offers grace to Ahaz even in his unbelief, extending an invitation to ask for any sign, and when Ahaz refuses under false humility, God still gives a sign, showing that His purposes of redemption do not depend on human cooperation or worthiness. God is also sovereign over international politics, using and later disciplining the very powers, Assyria, that faithless kings trust in place of Him.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 16:5-9 narrates the historical crisis behind this chapter, including Ahaz's fateful decision to appeal to Assyria for help. Matthew 1:22-23 explicitly cites Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled in the virgin birth of Jesus. Isaiah 8:8, 10 continues to address the child as Immanuel directly, reinforcing that the name marks God's ongoing presence even amid coming judgment. John 1:14 develops the fullest theological meaning of God dwelling, tabernacling, among His people in the incarnate Christ.
basic.oneStory: The sign of Immanuel given to faithless Ahaz previews the whole gospel pattern: God's presence and rescue given not because people ask rightly or deserve it, but because His mercy breaks through unbelief. That sign finds its full and final meaning in Jesus, God with us in the flesh, come to dwell among a people who, like Ahaz, so often refuse to trust Him.

context.literary:
Isaiah 7 is a narrative that carries its oracles inside it, and it is told in the third person, unlike chapter 6. It has a clear arc of three encounters at the same spot. In verses 1 to 9 the LORD sends Isaiah to Ahaz with a promise and a condition. In verses 10 to 17 the LORD speaks to Ahaz again, this time offering a sign, and Ahaz refuses. In verses 18 to 25 a series of 'on that day' sayings spells out what the refusal will cost. The chapter's pivot is the word 'Therefore' at the head of verse 14: because Ahaz will not ask, God will give.

The prose is full of heads and halves. Verse 8 is a little riddle of power, 'the head of Aram is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin,' and verse 9 repeats it for Ephraim, Samaria and the son of Remaliah, stopping each chain at a mere man. The point is that the great alliance is no more than a man at the top of a city. Against it stands the house of David, addressed in verses 2, 13 and 17, and whose last head is Ahaz, who is about to show how the chain of dependence ends.

The plural pronouns are important. 'You' in verse 13, and the 'you' to whom the sign is given in verse 14, are plural: the sign is for the house of David, not for Ahaz alone. The refrain 'on that day' in verses 18, 20, 21 and 23 turns the sign into a series of pictures, flies and bees, a razor, a single cow and two sheep, and briers where vines had stood. These are not a second prophecy but the same judgment seen from different angles.

The chapter sits within a larger structure, the so called book of Immanuel in chapters 7 to 12. Chapters 7 and 8 present the sign and the faithless king; chapter 9 gives the child born to the throne of David; chapter 11 the shoot from Jesse. Immanuel is first a sign in a crisis and then the key to the book's whole picture of a coming king.
context.historical:
The crisis is the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 735 to 732 BC. Rezin of Aram, whose capital was Damascus, and Pekah of Israel, the northern kingdom also called Ephraim, wanted Judah to join a coalition against the rising power of Assyria. When Ahaz would not, they marched on Jerusalem to remove him and put 'the son of Tabeal' on David's throne, verse 6. The aim was not conquest but replacement, and it threatened the Davidic line itself. 2 Kings 16:5 says that they besieged Ahaz but could not overcome him.

Isaiah meets Ahaz 'at the end of the aqueduct that feeds the upper pool,' verse 3, most likely where the king was inspecting Jerusalem's water supply in preparation for a siege. The same spot appears again in Isaiah 36:2, where Hezekiah's enemy, the Assyrian Rabshakeh, stands at the same aqueduct. A generation later, Ahaz's son faces at the same place the power his father invited. Ahaz's character comes out in 2 Kings 16:3 and 2 Chronicles 28:22-25: he sacrificed his own son in the fire, and in distress he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus.

Ahaz's real plan was to buy Assyria. 2 Kings 16:7-9 shows him sending messengers to Tiglath-pileser, calling himself 'your servant and your son,' and sending silver and gold taken from the temple and the palace. Assyria marched on Damascus and killed Rezin, and the two kings were removed. The Assyrian protection that Ahaz bought was a bargain with the empire that Isaiah says will turn on Judah. The 'razor hired from beyond the Euphrates' of verse 20 is the same Assyria Ahaz hired with temple silver, and in 2 Samuel 10:4-5 a shaved beard is a sign of public humiliation.

The 'sixty-five years' of verse 8 set a long horizon for the end of Ephraim as a people, and it is commonly connected with the resettlement of peoples in the north under later Assyrian kings, as Ezra 4:2 suggests. The nearer events came faster: Damascus fell in 732, and Samaria in about 722, 2 Kings 17:5-6.
context.canonical:
Immanuel is a thread that runs through Isaiah 7 to 12 and beyond. Isaiah 8:8 and 8:10 use the name in the middle of the flood of Assyria, 'O Immanuel,' and 'For God is with us.' The child of Isaiah 9:6-7, 'unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given,' will 'reign on the throne of David,' and is called 'Mighty God.' The shoot of Isaiah 11:1 grows from the stump of Jesse. Micah, who was a contemporary of Isaiah, links the birth of the ruler from Bethlehem to a woman in labor, Micah 5:2-3, and says that after her giving birth the rest of His brothers will return.

The birth announcements of earlier Scripture shape how the verse is heard. Genesis 16:11 and Judges 13:5 use the same formula, 'behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son,' for the births of Ishmael and Samson. It is the language of God announcing a child with a purpose and often a name.

In the New Testament, Matthew 1:22-23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled in the conception of Jesus by Mary, and explains that Immanuel means 'God with us.' Luke's annunciation, Luke 1:31-35, also draws on Isaiah 7 and 9, with its promise of the throne of David and a kingdom that never ends. At the end of Matthew the name returns as a promise, 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age,' Matthew 28:20, so that the Gospel is bracketed by Immanuel. In Revelation 21:3 the promise is completed: 'God Himself will be with them as their God.'

The call to faith in verse 9 is echoed by 2 Chronicles 20:20, 'Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld,' and takes the same two forms of the same verb. Paul's argument from Abraham, Genesis 15:6, 'Abram believed the LORD,' is the larger story in which Ahaz's refusal belongs.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted the house of David to see that the real issue in the crisis was not military but a matter of trust. He does not offer a defense plan. He gives Ahaz a command, 'Calm down and be quiet,' and a promise, 'It will not arise; it will not happen,' and then a condition that ties safety to faith, verse 9. Everything else in the chapter, the sign, the refusal, and the Assyrian devastation, is what follows from whether Ahaz believed.

The sign itself is meant to do two things at once. For Ahaz and his court it gives a time frame: before a child about to be born is old enough to tell right from wrong, the two kings will be gone. For those who have eyes to read, the name Immanuel gives the reason, God is with His people, and the child's birth into the house of David confirms that the Davidic line has not been cut off by the plot of verse 6. A child born to the royal house is the answer to a plot to end it.

Isaiah also meant his hearers to feel the irony of Ahaz's piety. The refusal to ask, 'I will not test the LORD,' sounds like obedience to Deuteronomy 6:16, but the LORD had commanded him to ask. His real trust is in the Assyrian king, and verses 18 to 25 show that the one he trusts will become the one who strips the land. The chapter's lesson for later readers is the cost of seeking security from a source other than God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what the LORD said to one king in one crisis. The sign is not a command for believers to demand signs, nor is Ahaz's refusal a model of humility. The text calls it a wearying of God, verse 13. The offer to ask for any sign is an unusual, king specific invitation and is not repeated as a standing promise for every anxious person.

What carries forward is the principle of verse 9, which the rest of Scripture repeats: security is found in believing the LORD, not in the alliances we arrange. That applies to nations, as in Isaiah 30:1-3 and 31:1, where the prophet warns against going down to Egypt for help, and to individuals who put their confidence in anything that will not bear it. It is also an encouragement. The God who gave a sign to a man who did not deserve one is the God who gives Himself, as Immanuel, to people who do not deserve Him. Where Scripture does apply the sign to Christ, Matthew 1:22-23, the application is made by an inspired author who saw the fuller meaning, and readers today follow him rather than invent their own.

debates.question: Who is the child of verse 14, and how does Matthew's use fit?

views.label: A child born in Isaiah's day, with a further fulfilment in Christ
views.case: The sign had to mean something to Ahaz, so the child is to be born within a few years, verses 15 and 16. Some propose a son of Ahaz, perhaps Hezekiah, others a son of Isaiah, like the sign child of Isaiah 8:3-4. Matthew then sees the pattern completed in Jesus. A difficulty with Hezekiah is chronology: 2 Kings 16:2 and 18:2 suggest that he was already born before the war. This view says Isaiah 7 holds a near fulfilment and a fuller one, with Matthew pointing to the second.

views.label: A prediction of the Messiah from the start
views.case: Because Isaiah 9:6-7 and 11:1-5 describe a child with divine titles on David's throne, some read Immanuel in the same line, and the near sign is the removal of the two kings as a pledge that this child will come. The plural 'you' in verse 14 points at the house of David as a whole, so the sign belongs to a long line of kings rather than a single nearby birth.

views.label: Typological fulfilment
views.case: Matthew uses the verb 'fulfil' in other places for patterns, as when he applies Hosea 11:1 to Jesus coming out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15. On this view the child in Isaiah's time was a real child and a type, and the full fulfilment is found in the one who is truly God with us.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that Matthew regards Jesus as the true Immanuel and that Isaiah's text carried a sign for Ahaz. The disagreement is about how many layers the original oracle held. A reader who sees Matthew's use as the work of the same Spirit can hold to either of the first two without losing the point that the name is finally filled out in Christ.

debates.question: Does 'almah' mean 'virgin'?

views.label: Young woman of marriageable age, and not a technical term for virgin
views.case: The word almah is used of Rebekah in Genesis 24:43, of Miriam in Exodus 2:8, and in the plural of the maidens in Song of Songs 1:3. The Hebrew word that most clearly means a virgin is bethulah, and Isaiah did not use it. The BSB footnote renders the alternative 'young woman.' The word describes a woman, and the context, not the term, tells us whether she is a virgin.

views.label: The context and the Greek translation support 'virgin'
views.case: In every Old Testament use the almah is an unmarried young woman, so 'virgin' is the natural sense of the people who used the word. The Greek translators of Isaiah chose parthenos, which is also the word in Matthew 1:23. Those translators lived centuries before Jesus, so the choice was not made to fit the Gospel.

views.label: The sign is that she is a woman who is pregnant, and the virgin birth rests on Matthew and Luke
views.case: The Hebrew says that the almah 'will be with child,' and the focus of Isaiah is the child's name and the timing, not the mother's history. The doctrine of the virginal conception rests on Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 1:34-35, which say plainly that Mary had not been with Joseph. On this view the word almah in Isaiah is open enough to allow the Gospel's fulfilment without making a doctrine depend on a single Hebrew word.

debates.bearing: The debate is real but should not be pitched as a choice between the Old Testament and the New. The Gospels affirm the virginal conception on their own testimony, and they read Isaiah 7:14 as pointing to it. The word 'virgin' in Matthew's quotation follows the Greek translation of Isaiah, and the Hebrew word is wide enough to be fulfilled in it.

study.originalLanguages:
The wordplay of verse 9 is finer than the English shows. 'If you do not stand firm in your faith, you will not stand at all' rests on two forms of one root, aman. The first verb, 'believe,' is in the active causative stem, to hold something as firm, and the second, 'be established,' is in the passive stem, to be made firm. Ahaz is told that the only way to be made firm is to treat God's word as firm, a sentence that sets human trust and divine support in one root. 2 Chronicles 20:20 repeats the pairing, and Genesis 15:6 uses the first form of the verb for Abraham. The 'you' who must believe is plural, the whole house of David.

The offer of verse 11 is wide: 'whether from the depths of Sheol or the heights of heaven.' The two extremes are the same pair Psalm 139:8 uses of God's presence, and the invitation puts no limit on what Ahaz may ask. The word for sign, oth, can mean a miracle, a token or a pledge, as with the rainbow in Genesis 9:12, and in Isaiah 8:18 the prophet and his children are called signs.

Verse 14 begins with hinneh, 'behold,' and then uses a pattern of words known from other birth announcements. The phrase 'is with child and will give birth to a son' has the same shape as the angel's words to Hagar, 'you have conceived and will bear a son,' Genesis 16:11, and to Samson's mother, Judges 13:5. The form means that the pregnancy is presented as a fact to be observed. The noun is ha-almah, with the definite article, 'the young woman,' which fits a particular woman known to speaker and hearer, or the representative figure of the sign. The verb 'will call' is, in the traditional Hebrew text, a feminine form, 'she will call,' as the BSB footnote notes; the footnote records that the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint read it differently, so the verb is a known variation in the textual tradition. The naming by the mother is a common feature of the Old Testament, as in Genesis 29 and 30.

The name Immanuel is built from three Hebrew parts: immanu, 'with us,' and el, 'God.' It is a sentence, a confession and a promise in one word. Isaiah 8:8 uses it as a direct address, 'O Immanuel,' showing that the child's name is also the land's name, and verse 10 of the same chapter gives the same name as the reason to be unafraid.

The child 'knows enough to reject evil and choose good' in verses 15 and 16, literally knows to refuse the evil and choose the good. Isaiah 8:4 gives a parallel age mark, when the boy can cry 'Father' or 'Mother.' Both are rough timeframes of a few years.

The name Shear-jashub, 'a remnant will return,' in verse 3, which the BSB footnote explains, is a message in the form of a child: a name that already holds judgment and hope. 'Curds and honey' in verses 15 and 22 are the food of a land stripped of farming, since a farmer with no grain lives on what cattle and bees provide, as verses 21 and 22 show. They can sound like plenty, but they are the diet of a land after judgment.

typology.fulfillment: The name given as a sign to Ahaz becomes the identity of Christ. Matthew applies Isaiah 7:14 to Jesus and translates the name, 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23. The correspondence is between a promised child of David's house whose existence signals God's presence, and Jesus, in whom 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. The escalation is that the child in Isaiah's day signified God's help; Jesus is that help in person. The type falls short because the first Immanuel announced a presence that did not save Ahaz, while Christ's presence is accompanied by 'I am with you always,' Matthew 28:20.

typology.type: The faithless son of David and the faithful one
typology.fulfillment: Ahaz is a son of David who refuses to trust God, and who covers his refusal in pious words. His answer, 'I will not test the LORD,' quotes the principle of Deuteronomy 6:16 while ignoring a direct command. Jesus is tempted to put God to the test and answers with that same verse, Matthew 4:5-7, and obeys it where Ahaz only recited it. The correspondence is between two heirs of David facing a crisis and a decision to trust. The escalation is that Jesus, 'the Son of the Most High,' is given the throne of David, Luke 1:32, and does what Ahaz would not. The pattern is a contrast more than a likeness.

A child whose name is a promise, 'a remnant will return,' walks beside Isaiah to meet the king. The remnant thought returns throughout Isaiah and is taken up by Paul in Romans 9:27, 'only the remnant will be saved,' and Romans 11:5, 'a remnant chosen by grace.' The correspondence is the survival of a few by God's choice when the many fall. The escalation is the Messiah as the one remnant in whom all the faithful are gathered, and the Church as the people He gathers from every nation. The type is limited in that Shear-jashub's name is a sign of national survival, while the New Testament fulfilment reaches beyond Israel.

What Ahaz thought was protection becomes the instrument of shame. The pattern of trusting an earthly power rather than God and being undone by that power appears again in Isaiah 30:1-3, where Egypt's protection becomes Judah's shame. In Christ the pattern is reversed: those who take refuge in Him are not put to shame, Romans 9:33. The type falls short because the razor is an image of judgment and not a picture of Christ, but it shows what looking elsewhere for refuge costs, and why Christ is the only refuge that holds.

study.christ:
Matthew places Isaiah 7:14 at the head of his Gospel. After the angel tells Joseph that Mary's child is conceived by the Holy Spirit, Matthew says, 'All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet,' and quotes the verse, adding, 'which means, God with us,' Matthew 1:22-23. The choice of this text is deliberate. Matthew's Gospel will close with Jesus saying, 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age,' Matthew 28:20, so that the whole book is held between the promise of Immanuel at the beginning and its fulfilment at the end. For Matthew, to meet Jesus is to meet God with us.

The chapter leads to Christ by pattern. A threat to the throne of David, a faithless king, and a child as the sign of God's faithfulness set the stage for the coming of the greater son of David. Isaiah 9:6-7 develops the sign: the child is born 'unto us,' will carry the government on His shoulders, will be called 'Mighty God,' and will reign on David's throne 'with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore.' Luke's announcement to Mary echoes the language, 'The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever,' Luke 1:32-33. Whatever fulfilment Isaiah's immediate hearers saw, the full measure of the child belongs to Jesus.

It leads to Christ by contrast. Ahaz refuses a sign and would not ask the LORD for help. Jesus is the sign given to a people who did not ask. 'God with us' is not a reward for their faith, and Simeon says that this child 'is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be spoken against,' Luke 2:34. The one who is the presence of God comes to the very house that, in Ahaz's day, tried His patience, and in Jesus's day was often unwilling to receive Him.

The faith that verse 9 asks for is the faith the New Testament calls for in Christ. 'The one who believes in Him will never be put to shame,' Romans 9:33, speaks of the same stability that Isaiah promises to those who stand firm in their trust. The danger Ahaz faced, relying on the wrong source of safety, is the danger the gospel addresses.

A word of care. The virginal conception is taught by Matthew and Luke on their own account, and we do not need to prove it from the Hebrew of Isaiah alone. The curds and honey, the razor, and the briers are not coded references to Jesus's childhood or ministry. What the New Testament takes from the chapter is the sign and the name, and the pattern of the faithless and faithful sons of David. The links rest on what Matthew and Luke say and on the way Isaiah's own later chapters develop the child.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who commands calm in a crisis. Isaiah's first word to Ahaz is not rebuke but comfort: 'Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened,' verse 4. The kings who seem so fearsome are 'smoldering stubs of firewood,' burned out torches. God sees the real size of the powers that terrify His people, and He measures them by Himself, not by their armies. The chain 'head of Aram is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin' in verse 8 reduces an empire to a man.

He is patient with the unbelieving. Ahaz has already shown that he is a faithless king, yet the LORD comes to him a second time, 'Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz,' verse 10, and offers the widest possible sign, from Sheol to heaven. The offer is generous to the point of extravagance. Even when Ahaz refuses, God does not withdraw but gives a sign Himself. The language of verse 14, 'the Lord Himself will give you a sign,' stresses that the initiative rests with God when humans will not take it.

He is also truthful about the cost of unbelief. The word that is a promise to those who believe is a warning to those who do not, verse 9. The 'Assyria' of verse 17 is spoken of as something the LORD Himself brings: 'The LORD will bring on you... the king of Assyria.' Verse 18 pictures Him whistling for flies and bees, and verse 20 calls Assyria a razor He hires. Judgment is not an accident of politics but the working of the God who rules the nations, and who can use the instrument Ahaz chose as His own. This is not a God who is surprised by history. At the same time, the responsibility for the choice lies fully with Ahaz, who was offered another way.

The name Immanuel gives the chapter's central statement about God. The God of Israel is not remote. He commits to be with His people in danger, in judgment, and in the long run in flesh. Isaiah 8:10, 'For God is with us,' says the same name as a defiance of every plan against His people. A doctrine of God that held only His transcendence would not account for this; the chapter holds His rule over empires and His nearness to a frightened household together.

He keeps His promises to David. The plot to depose the house of David in verse 6 will not succeed, because of the covenant made in 2 Samuel 7. In a situation in which the dynasty looked finished, God points to a child as proof that it is not.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to bring fear to God before we bring it to alliances. The right response to a threat is not the one Ahaz made, but the stand of verse 9. It also teaches us to receive the name Immanuel not only as a doctrine but as a promise, in the words of Psalm 46:7, 'The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.'

crossReferences.note: The historical account of the same crisis. Rezin and Pekah besiege Ahaz and cannot overcome him; Ahaz sends temple silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser, who takes Damascus. It shows Ahaz taking the Assyrian route that Isaiah warned against, and explains the 'razor hired from beyond the Euphrates' of verse 20.

The Rabshakeh stands at the aqueduct of the upper pool on the road to the Launderer's Field, the same spot where Isaiah met Ahaz in Isaiah 7:3. The place binds the two crises together: Ahaz's refusal to trust and Hezekiah's later test, in which the Assyrian power Ahaz invited comes to Jerusalem's gate.

Jehoshaphat tells Judah, 'Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld.' The two verbs are forms of the same root as Isaiah 7:9, so it reads like an echo or a quotation of the principle. A king who obeys it is the opposite of Ahaz.

Rebekah is called an almah when Abraham's servant stands at the spring. It is one of the clearest uses of the word and shows it describes a young woman of marriageable age. The context of Genesis 24:16 describes her as a virgin, which suggests that the word fits a woman of that kind though it does not itself say so.

The angel announces to Samson's mother, 'you will conceive and give birth to a son,' with the same pattern as Isaiah 7:14 and Genesis 16:11. It shows that a birth announcement with a purpose was a recognised form, and that the child's role is given with the promise of his birth.

The name Immanuel returns in the next chapter, first as the land that the Assyrian flood overruns and then as the reason the plots of the nations will fail, 'For God is with us.' It shows that the child of chapter 7 is not a passing sign but a name that holds through judgment.

The child born to the throne of David is given the titles Wonderful Counselor and Mighty God, and His government will have no end. It answers the threat of Isaiah 7:6 against the house of David by promising a ruler who cannot be deposed. Read with Isaiah 7:14, it supports hearing Immanuel as a Messianic name.

Matthew tells the conception of Jesus through the Holy Spirit and cites Isaiah 7:14 for it. He gives the fuller story of what the sign meant: Joseph is told not to be afraid, as Ahaz was, and Jesus is given the name that means 'He will save His people from their sins.' The faith that Ahaz refused is shown in Joseph.

Gabriel's announcement to Mary uses the pattern of Isaiah 7:14 and 9:6-7, the conception, the son, the throne of David and a kingdom without end. Mary's question about how it can be and the angel's answer about the Holy Spirit show the Gospel's own account of the virginal conception, which stands alongside Matthew's use of Isaiah.

Jesus answers the devil's suggestion that He test God with 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test.' It is the verse that Ahaz used as a cover, Deuteronomy 6:16, and Jesus keeps it in the sense it was meant. The contrast between the two sons of David is sharp.

A later woe against those who go down to Egypt for help without asking the LORD. It repeats the lesson of Isaiah 7 in another generation: shelter sought from the wrong power becomes shame. It shows that Ahaz's mistake was a recurring habit of Judah's rulers.

The last words of Matthew's Gospel, 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age,' close the circle that Matthew opened with Immanuel in Matthew 1:23. The promise of God's presence moves from a name to a commission, and shows that the name is a lasting reality for the Church.

study.oneStory:
The chapter picks up a story that began with a promise to David. In 2 Samuel 7 God said that David's house and throne would be established forever, and when the kingdom split after Solomon, the line continued in Judah, 1 Kings 12:16-20. By Isaiah's day the promise looked fragile. Two kings plotted to end the line, and the reigning king was a man who sacrificed his son and bought protection with the temple's silver. Isaiah 7 shows that the covenant does not depend on the strength or faithfulness of the king. God keeps the line alive because of His word.

The chapter also continues the theme of faith. In Genesis 15:6 Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness. From the beginning of the story, standing in the covenant has meant trusting what God says. Ahaz is the opposite of Abraham: offered a sign beyond any limit, he declines, and the one who would not stand firm in faith will not stand at all. The same principle runs through the later prophets and into the New Testament, where Paul builds his argument for justification on the same Genesis verse.

What follows in Isaiah is the long unfolding of the child. Chapter 8 names Assyria's flood and repeats the name, chapter 9 describes the child born to the throne, chapter 11 shows the shoot from Jesse's stump, and the later chapters speak of a Servant who will suffer and bring justice. The exile that Isaiah warns about is the setting for these promises, which grow clearer as the line of David seems to fail.

The New Testament says where the story arrives. A child is born in David's town to a virgin, the angel promises the throne of David and a kingdom without end, and the name Immanuel is given to Jesus. His death and resurrection overcome the enemy whose power Ahaz feared, and His promise to be with His people to the end of the age makes the name Immanuel a present reality.

The new creation is the final fulfilment of the name. In Revelation 21:3 a loud voice says, 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.' The sign that began in a conduit outside Jerusalem ends in a city with no temple, because God Himself is its dwelling. The threat to David's throne and the briers of the stripped land are gone, and the God who is with us is with us for good.

quiz.q: Why were Ahaz and his people so terrified according to verses 1-2?

options.text: Aram and Israel had allied together to attack Jerusalem and replace Ahaz with a puppet king.
options.note: This is the Syro-Ephraimite crisis, a real, historical political and military threat.

options.text: A plague had broken out in Jerusalem.
options.note: The threat described is a military coalition, not disease.

options.text: Assyria had already conquered Judah.
options.note: Assyria's devastation is warned about later in the chapter as a future consequence, not yet an accomplished conquest.

options.text: Uzziah had just died, leaving no heir.
options.note: Uzziah's death is the setting of chapter 6; here Ahaz, his grandson, is already reigning and threatened by the Aram-Israel coalition.

quiz.q: How does Ahaz respond when invited to ask God for any sign he wants?

options.text: He refuses, dressing his unbelief up as pious reluctance to test the LORD.
options.note: Isaiah exposes this as trying the patience of God, not genuine humility.

options.text: He eagerly asks for a sign from the depths of Sheol.
options.note: Ahaz explicitly refuses to ask for any sign at all.

options.text: He asks Isaiah to consult other prophets instead.
options.note: The text records a direct refusal, not a request for alternate counsel.

options.text: He accepts but demands a delay of several years.
options.note: Ahaz's response is an outright refusal, not a request for delay.

quiz.q: What does the name Immanuel mean, and why is it significant?

options.text: God with us, a name that ultimately identifies Jesus Christ Himself as God dwelling among His people.
options.note: Matthew 1:23 explicitly translates and applies this name directly to Christ.

options.text: It means mighty warrior and refers only to a future military leader.
options.note: The name's actual meaning is God with us, not a military title.

options.text: It is simply a common name with no theological significance.
options.note: The name is theologically loaded throughout Isaiah 7-8 and climactically in Matthew's Gospel.

options.text: It refers exclusively to the return from Babylonian exile.
options.note: While some see a near fulfillment in Isaiah's own day, the name's fullest, New Testament-confirmed meaning centers on Christ's incarnation.

quiz.q: What irony does the chapter's ending reveal about Ahaz's unbelief?

options.text: The very Assyrian power Ahaz would later turn to for help would instead devastate his own land.
options.note: 2 Kings 16:7-9 records Ahaz's actual appeal to Assyria, which brought long-term subjugation rather than lasting rescue.

options.text: Aram and Israel eventually became Judah's permanent allies.
options.note: The text says these two kings and their threat would come to nothing, not that they became allies.

options.text: Judah's population grew dramatically as a result of Ahaz's decisions.
options.note: The described outcome is devastation, briers, and thorns, not population growth.

options.text: Ahaz eventually repented and trusted the LORD fully.
options.note: The historical record and this chapter's warnings suggest ongoing faithlessness rather than full repentance.

quiz.q: What does verse 9's wordplay, if you do not stand firm, you will not be established, emphasize?

options.text: That trust in God is itself the very foundation of genuine stability and security.
options.note: The shared Hebrew root ties belief and stability together linguistically and theologically.

options.text: That military strength alone determines a nation's survival.
options.note: The verse ties survival to faith, not to military might.

options.text: That Ahaz's political alliances would guarantee Judah's safety.
options.note: The verse challenges reliance on political maneuvering, calling instead for trust in God.

options.text: That prophecy always requires a visible sign to be believed.
options.note: The verse is a call to trust apart from demanding proof, the opposite of requiring visible confirmation first.

questions: Ahaz refused to ask God for a sign, dressing unbelief up as piety. Where might you be avoiding trust in God under the guise of not wanting to 'test' Him?
God gave the sign of Immanuel even though Ahaz refused to ask for it. How does it change you to know that God's promises do not depend on your asking rightly or deserving them?

Ahaz eventually turned to Assyria instead of trusting the LORD, and that choice brought long-term trouble he was trying to avoid. What 'Assyria' are you tempted to lean on instead of trusting God right now?
The name Immanuel, God with us, was first a sign of comfort in crisis. Where do you most need to remember that God is genuinely with you in your present fear or uncertainty?
Verse 9 ties standing firm to believing firmly. What would it look like this week to let your trust in God, rather than your circumstances, be the ground of your stability?

translationNotes.note: The wordplay ta'aminu, you believe or stand firm, and te'amenu, you will be established, both from the same root aman, is largely untranslatable into English, though several versions attempt it with phrases like 'stand firm... not stand at all.'

Almah denotes a young woman of marriageable age, generally presumed unmarried and thus a virgin in the cultural context, though it is not the more technical Hebrew term betulah; the Septuagint's Greek translators nonetheless rendered it parthenos, virgin, centuries before Christ, and Matthew 1:23 follows that translation in applying it to Mary.

The imagery of a hired razor shaving head, legs, and beard pictures total, humiliating devastation, since shaving in this culture, apart from specific rituals, was associated with shame and mourning, and here it symbolizes Assyria stripping Judah bare.
